## Data load and preparation before modelling

```{r read_data}
gss16<-read.csv("data/gss16.csv")
```

#### Cleaning and selecting columns

```{r}
gss16_advfront <- gss16 %>%
  select(advfront, emailhr, educ, polviews, wrkstat) %>%
  drop_na()
```

#### Re-levelling `advfront`

```{r}
gss16_advfront <- gss16_advfront %>%
  mutate(
    advfront = case_when(
      advfront == "Strongly agree" ~ "Agree",
      advfront == "Agree" ~ "Agree",
      TRUE ~ "Not agree"
    ),
    advfront = fct_relevel(advfront, "Not agree", "Agree")
  )
```

#### Re-levelling `polviews`

```{r}
gss16_advfront <- gss16_advfront %>%
  mutate(
    polviews = case_when(
      str_detect(polviews, "[Cc]onservative") ~ "Conservative",
      str_detect(polviews, "[Ll]iberal") ~ "Liberal",
      TRUE ~ polviews
    ),
    polviews = fct_relevel(polviews, "Conservative", "Moderate", "Liberal")
  )
```


## Exercise 1: Create a linear regression model

#### Exercise 1 (a)

```{r}
gss16_linear <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(emailhr ~ educ, data = gss16_advfront)

tidy(gss16_linear)

```

The formula for the line-of-best-fit is emailhr = -2.757 + 0.685 x educ. The interpretation of this estimate is that for each extra year of education level a person has, the number of hours they spend on email in a week increases by 0.685 hours. The intercept does not have a meaningful interpretation because someone cannot spend -2.757 hours on email. 

#### Exercise 1 (b)

```{r}
glance(gss16_linear)

ggplot(data = gss16_advfront, aes(x = educ, y = emailhr)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Education Level vs. Time Spent on Email in a Week",
    subtitle = "General Social Survey",
    x = "Education Level (years)",
    y = "Time Spent on Email in a Week (hours)"
  )
```

The linear regression model does not perform well in this case. The R-squared value is 0.29, from which we can deduce that only 29% of the variation in emailhr can be explained by educ in this model. There is a pattern of points being clumped together in vertical lines in the scatter plot, which the linear model does not explain. Instead, the equation of the line-of-best-fit creates the false illusion of a linear correlation between the explanatory and response variable.

## Exercise 2: Create a workflow to fit a model

```{r split-data}
set.seed(1234)
gss16_split <- initial_split(gss16_advfront)
gss16_train <- training(gss16_split)
gss16_test  <- testing(gss16_split)
```

#### Exercise 2 (a)

```{r}

gss16_rec_1 <- recipe(
  advfront ~ educ,
  data = gss16_train
)

summary(gss16_rec_1)

gss16_mod_1 <- logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm")

gss16_wflow_1 <- workflow () %>%
  add_model(gss16_mod_1) %>%
  add_recipe(gss16_rec_1)


  
```

```{r}
```

I chose a logistic regression for this model because we are using the numerical predictor educ to predict the binary categorical outcome of advfront, which is either "Agree" or "Not Agree". Since we are predicting this binary outcome, it does not make sense to use a different type of regression such as a linear model.

#### Exercise 2 (c)


## Exercise 3: Logistic regression with single predictor

#### Exercise 3 (a)

```{r}
gss16_pred <- predict(gss16_fit_1, gss16_test, type = "prob") %>%
  bind_cols(gss16_test %>% select(advfront, educ))

gss16_pred

gss16_pred %>%
  roc_curve(
    truth = advfront,
    .pred_Agree,
    event_level = "second"
  ) %>%
  autoplot()
```

*Your answer here*

#### Exercise 3 (b)

```{r}

library(knitr)

cutoff_prob <- 0.83
gss16_pred %>%
  mutate(
    advfront = if_else(advfront == "Agree", "Agreed", "Disagreed"),
    advfront_pred = if_else(.pred_Agree > cutoff_prob, "Predicted to have agreed", "Predicted to have disagreed")
    ) %>%
      count(advfront_pred, advfront) %>%
      pivot_wider(names_from = advfront, values_from = n) %>%
      kable(col.names = c("", "Agreed", "Disagreed"))

sensitivity <- 147/(147+118)
specificity <- 18/(10+18)

sensitivity
specificity

```

The sensitivity is 0.555 and the specificity is 0.643.

#### Exercise 4 (c) 

```{r}
#Calculating specificity and sensitivity for this model

cutoff_prob <- 0.83
gss16_pred2 %>%
  mutate(
    advfront = if_else(advfront == "Agree", "Agreed", "Disagreed"),
    advfront_pred = if_else(.pred_Agree > cutoff_prob, "Predicted to have agreed", "Predicted to have disagreed")
    ) %>%
      count(advfront_pred, advfront) %>%
      pivot_wider(names_from = advfront, values_from = n) %>%
      kable(col.names = c("", "Agreed", "Disagreed"))

sensitivity <- 177/(177+88)
specificity <- 11/(11+17)

sensitivity
specificity

#Calculating the area under the curve for model 1:

gss16_pred %>%
  roc_auc(
    truth = advfront,
    .pred_Agree,
    event_level = "second"
  )


```

After having calculated the sensitivity, specificity, and area under the ROC curves for both models, it is safe to say that model 1 shows better performance. Model 1 has a specificity of 0.643, whereas model 2 has a specificity of 0.393. This shows that model 1 has a much lower false negative rate than model 2, which shows that its predictions are more accurate. Moreover, looking at the ROC curves, the AUC for model 1 is 0.581 and the AUC for model 2 is 0.535. When looking at the ROC, the AUC should be as close to 1 as possible, since that indicates better model performance and higher accuracy in making predictions. The only statistic that acts as a weakness for model 1 is its lower sensitivity (0.555) in comparison to model 2 (0.668). However, the difference is minor and likely does not take any from model 1's accuracy.
